Chapter 10—Carrying the Aftertaste: What Remains
Leaving Russia—whether it’s just for a week or forever—is never as simple as packing your bags and saying goodbye. The flavors, the stories, even the little habits you pick up around someone’s kitchen table... they all seem to follow you home. There’s this lingering aftertaste to Russian life. It’s sweet, it’s complicated—a mix of memories, gratitude, and maybe a touch of longing.
So, imagine landing back in your own country. Suddenly, you’re craving things you never thought you’d miss—like the slow simmer of borscht filling your kitchen, flipping blini on a lazy Sunday morning, or lining up jars of pickles along the window. Cooking becomes more than just making dinner. It’s your way of holding onto the past, keeping those connections alive.
Friends start gathering, curious about these new dishes you’re sharing. And before you know it, you’re telling stories—about snowy streets, neighbors who went out of their way for you, and those quiet, magical moments of Russian hospitality.
What’s surprising is how those little lessons stick. Sharing, lingering over a meal, opening your door to others—suddenly, it’s all second nature. Where you were once the guest, now you’re the host, passing on those rituals of warmth and generosity to everyone around you.
Of course, there are moments when nostalgia sneaks up on you—a familiar song on the radio, the scent of fresh dill, or the memory of laughter bouncing off the walls of a tiny kitchen. But instead of just reminding you of what you’ve left behind, these moments show you how much you’ve gained. Living in Russia, learning its rhythms and its rituals, leaves a mark you can’t quite shake off.
Most of us don’t realize just how much we carry from the places we’ve called home. But, looking back, it becomes clear—the real aftertaste isn’t just in the food. It’s in how you move through life now—with a little more patience, a bit more openness, and a whole new appreciation for what it means to simply share a meal.
